The page on a socket: one morph per block, proven on the wire

Package 2's web slice. The rung has been claiming that the morph target
is the block; this is the first time that claim is measured where it
matters, on a real socket, and it holds:

  initial paint            2 patches, 218 bytes  (one per block)
  commit changing one block 1 patch,  102 bytes  (banner never sent)
  commit changing nothing   0 patches,   0 bytes

The quarry sent the entire <main id="app-view"> subtree on any relevant
datom. Every one of those three rows is a sealed test against a real
http-kit server on an ephemeral loopback port, not a mocked handler —
a handler called as a function proves the derivation and leaves the
claim untested.

WHAT IS REAL: the server, the routes, the shell, initial paint, live
repaint driven by listen!, per-block equality suppression comparing
BYTES, the latest-wins mailbox, and the coalescing floor as a config
fact. WHAT IS NOT is enumerated in `not-yet` rather than implied by
silence — interest matching, the shared registration, the per-tab flow
graph, the isolated sink. Each has a settled design and none is an open
question; a feed that quietly did less than the design says would be
the absence-read-as-health class on the most visible surface we have.

The listener does almost nothing and that is a hard constraint, not a
style: Datahike invokes it on the writer's commit path, so it offers
onto the mailbox and returns. Painting happens on the connection's own
virtual thread. Its lifetime is the socket's, so a departed tab leaves
nothing behind — sealed by hammering the writer after a close.

THREE BUGS THE INSTRUMENTS CAUGHT, all mine:

The first live page came back 15 bytes — just the doctype. `page`
returns a VECTOR OF ELEMENTS, which is not hiccup as a child, and the
grammar refused the whole document rather than emitting something
plausible. It needed `seq`, and `page`'s docstring now says so. That
refusal is a feature; a serializer that guessed would have shipped a
subtly wrong page.

Then the SSE proof reported zero events for a feed that was working:
BodyHandlers/ofLines does not yield on a stream that never ends. Then
it reported the PREVIOUS paint as the current one, because one .read
returns one chunk — which briefly looked like a suppression bug in the
server. Reading SSE correctly is now part of the test, with both traps
written down where the next person will hit them.

The feed opener is a hidden SIBLING of the surfaces, and there is a test
for it: a data-init inside a morphed element is stripped by that
element's first whole-element morph, and the tab then looks alive while
receiving nothing. The quarry paid for that lesson.

A require refused for closing a namespace cycle answers its refusal; it no longer returns nil with the alias silently dropped (S5 run 4)

Reproduced on agent branch require-alias (MCP eval_clj, SCI mode):
- in-ns seon.error: (require '[clojure.string :as cs]) (cs/upper-case "a") -> "A",
  in the same request and the next. (require '[clojure.pprint :as pp]) also adds pp.
  So library requires were already fine; this commit's first two table rows were green on HEAD.
- (require '[seon.test-support :as test-support]) in seon.error -> :value nil, no alias,
  no error, in every request. Inside one form, (do (require ...) (ns-aliases *ns*)) shows
  the alias: SCI adds it, and then the facts stage takes it away.

Cause: seon.turn.batch/form-facts finds that the require closes a cycle
(seon.test-support requires seon.error), and refuse-cycle! takes the alias out of SCI
and returns the refusal as the form's facts-error. seon.turn/evaluate-sources passed
that refusal on (not-admitted) only when the form bound a Var or registered a schema.
That condition was a filter (4be90d597) added to hide namespace-only refusals of plain
calls, and a bare require binds neither, so it was dropped silently. Run 4's first
attempt saw the refusal only because its form also had a def.

Fix: remove the filter. Every facts-error is delivered beside its value, and the
registered? binding it used is deleted. The plain-call regression
(a-plain-failing-call-never-carries-the-not-admitted-diagnostic) stays green, so the
spurious refusal it guarded against no longer comes out of the facts stage. The cycle
refusal message now says the require adds no alias, and where to require from instead.

Decision (spec gap): a cycle-closing REPL require is refused with an error value rather
than honoured. Clojure would honour it at the REPL because the namespace is already
loaded, but the program's namespace declarations would then be cyclic and the files
could not load.

seon.instrument is small because the composition was already built: on
:panic the reporter THROWS our own flat :seon.instrument/contract-violated
value, and when that throw happens inside a flow proc it is a Throwable
escaping our code onto ::flow/error — so an instrumentation violation
becomes a durable error fact, an explanation message and a `problems`
entry through the path step 2 wired. Nothing here had to know that.

The selection is COMPUTED — every loaded public var carrying
:malli/schema — which excludes every hot inner walker BY CONSTRUCTION,
because they are all defn- without schemas. No prefix, no exclusion
list. Measured cost stays where it belongs: +129ns on a two-int call,
+175ns on a closed map arg, per instrumented BOUNDARY call.

:record instruments nothing and removes what is there (judgment,
flagged): report mode cannot prevent the bad call — measured, the call
still runs and throws naturally a moment later — it taxes every public
boundary ~150ns forever, and the natural failure still becomes a fault
through the wired channel. Reversible in one line if the owner wants
violations NAMED in production rather than diagnosed from consequences.

and the evidence said no: every test that boots a cluster then
instruments the whole JVM, so a suite's result depends on whether an
earlier suite happened to boot one — and a CLUSTER-scoped dial silently
mutating PROCESS-global var roots is the wrong seam anyway. The dev loop
is where a human is watching. The suite's own fixture removes
instrumentation in a `finally` for the same reason.

FOUR CONTRACTS WERE WRONG, and every one had never been checked because
nothing had ever compiled them:

1. seon.schema/projection-delta bound two arguments to one :catn name.
   :catn refuses duplicate keys, so the contract could not compile —

2. seon.cluster/root-executors inlined [:fn seon.flow/executor?]. A
   :malli/schema goes straight to malli, which has no resolver for a
   bare symbol. The shape is now registered once (:seon.boot/executors)
   and referenced by both the instance and the fn — the rule about
   registering shared shapes exists for exactly this.
3. :seon.cluster.loop/cluster did not admit ::flow/pid, which flow adds
   to a proc's args map (flow/impl.clj:155). The contract was wrong
   about its own live input.
4. :seon.cluster.loop/turn-report required a run id that an :open turn

   the contract was wrong about its most common report.

(right answer, wrong question), and the instance now holds a

An interrupted run reaps the child it admitted, and reports the interruption

Three failures at one seam, from the tool-exercise lane: sleep 300 was still
running 29 s after its run was cut at a 4 s limit, its effect receipt was
permanently pending, and the eval receipt carried a contract violation from
the code that was trying to record the problem.

The child outlived its evaluation because two limits govern a foreground
child and only one was observed. The shell waited on
:seon.config.shell/time-limit-ms; the arm's deadline is the limit that
ADMITTED the work, and a thread parked in a host call makes no interpreted
function entrance, so SCI's interrupt could never reach it. The arm now
carries its deadline as a value and publishes it — kernel/deadline-remaining-ms
and deadline-reached? — which is the interface change the timeout rule asks
for: rather than bolting a second clock onto a handler, blocking work asks
the one deadline that already exists. await-exit waits on whichever limit
ends first and returns which one it was, so no arm of the handler can return
while its child is alive. The receipt terminates with the process because
both arms return :seon.effect/disposition :interrupted, which is what
seon.effect already stamps :seon.effect/interrupted-at from.

:seon.sci.eval/evaluation: the submission backstop hand-built four keys of a
value with nine required ones, so its own report reached
seon.problems/form-problem missing :seon.cluster.eval/ns,

Compile a declaration against its predicate's source, not this JVM's copy

A long-lived JVM holds the copy of a namespace it loaded at boot. Schema
resources are read from the classpath on every publication, so a commit that
adds a predicate AND the [:fn ...] declaration naming it makes the
declaration live instantly while the loaded namespace still lacks the
predicate. `loaded-predicate-var` then resolves nothing and the publication
is refused — including the publication whose own adoption would have reloaded
the owner. `default` was wedged this way for every agent by
`seon.search/handle?`: the branch publication of current-src refused with
:seon.schema/unresolved-predicate at the scratch schema transaction, and no
edit could ever converge it. Its sibling predicates resolve only because they
predate the JVM's load; privacy is irrelevant, `ns-resolve` returns a private
Var. A fresh JVM compiles the same commit without complaint.

That is the pre-read the owner law forbids: the var table is a MIRROR of the
source the publication is about to re-decide. `converged-predicate-var` now
reloads an ALREADY-LOADED namespace whose source declares a predicate its
loaded copy does not have — the only thing that replays its
register-core-predicate! forms, since `require` on a loaded namespace is a
no-op. An unloaded namespace is left alone and still refuses, so an authored
[:fn ...] still cannot make the process require code. Convergence runs only
where the alternative is the refusal itself, so it can turn a wedge into a
success and cannot change a working compile, and it remembers nothing: a memo
would be the process-global predicate state
one-predicate-symbol-cannot-name-two-environments-callables forbids, and that
regression caught the first draft holding one. A surviving refusal now names
:seon.schema/predicate-namespace as well as the predicate.

The class regression ns-unmaps a loaded probe namespace's declared predicate —
the live state exactly — proves a plain require cannot leave it, proves
compilation converges, and proves an unloaded namespace is still never
required.

Refork holds no store across the arm that releases it, and exists once

Two defects, one hidden behind the other.

GUESSED its operator inputs — the managed root two parents up from the
cluster root, the repository root from a system property. Off the

a forced refork of the only cluster in a JVM destroyed the old branch and
failed to fork the new one. Each arm now acquires its own store.

real store in the operator's layout with a real claim, printing the

Close the eval seam: one ctx per run, the deadline as a dial, R41 reversed

Three bundled rulings, and the seam my last report flagged is gone.

1. THE SEAM FIX. `turn`'s :resume is now the FOLD, not one form: it
   forks ONE ctx per run and threads it through every form, so a plan
   reads like a REPL session — form 2 sees what form 1 defined. sci's
   fork copies the env, so a ctx per form loses defs; that was the
   State A defect. The deadline rides the cluster handle from a real
   dial: :seon.config.eval/time-limit-ms, registered in config.edn with
   manifest/effective/entity rows and a provenanced 30000 ms in
   config/default.edn — three orders of magnitude above the measured
   ~55 ms interrupt latency and still well under human patience. The
   config suite's dial set and model attributes grow with it.
   A kill mid-fold loses the ctx, so a resumed fold starts fresh and
   later forms may not resolve earlier defs. That is the crash model
   working — nothing re-executes and the agent is told — and it is
   stated at the call site rather than papered over.
2. R41 REVERSES THE ADMISSION TASTE CALL. A value the total codec
   cannot project is a core degradation, not agent input, so the dial
   decides: :panic throws hard and loud (a hole in OUR codec must be
   found immediately), :record degrades to the marker plus a
   best-effort description — never a deref, never anything sequential
   (`str` on a lazy sequence realizes it), always truncated. The dial
   is a required key on both the admit and evaluate requests: a caller
   that has not decided has not thought about it, and a schema test
   proves the request without it is invalid.
   Writing the acceptance for this found something: a bare Seqable is
   NOT hostile to the codec, because the walk never enters it. The test
   uses a collection whose `seq` throws, which is the real failure path.
3. `interrupted?` HAS ONE OWNER. admit.clj asks seon.sci.eval rather
   than keeping a copy.

New `seon.db.relay` ns: per-agent Nippy/TCP server (orchestrator) and
client (agent JVM) over the existing `seon.flow.harness.channel` adapter.
On `seon.session/launch!` we open one relay server per agent, hand its
port to the bootstrap, and the agent connects back. The bootstrap
interns shim fns into `seon.db` (transact!, query, pull-by-name,
pull-many-by-name) that route through the relay — so agent code reads
as `(seon.db/transact! :seon.orchestrator [...])` and works without
the agent JVM needing the heavy `seon.db` deps (integrant/datahike are
deliberately absent from `:agent` alias).

Orchestrator-side `seon.db` gains a relay-active? branch in each op:
the orchestrator never sets `*relay-active?*`, so its dispatch is
unchanged. The relay-server dispatches to `seon.db/<op>` directly,
which then routes through the datahike flow as normal.

Lifecycle: relay-server is created before spawn so the bootstrap can
hand the agent a valid port; closed on `stop!` (and on launch failure).

Why a separate Integrant key was NOT used: relay servers are
per-agent, not system-wide, so they're owned by the session lifecycle.
A system-level key would either need an accept-loop wrapper around the
single-client `harness.channel` (extra surface area) or a way to track
N transient sub-resources by id — both worse than the per-agent model.

- the bare default then runs ONLY the tests reaching code changed since the

  modification time, a filename convention, or a maintained list;
- `--all` keeps the old non-long sweep, `--full` the complete suite,
  `--platform` the moving parts alone, `--changed PATH` an explicit
  selection, and an explicit namespace selection still runs every test in
  those namespaces.

the gate runs before any cluster exists and its own run-root store is
deleted on success, so there is no database home for it yet. It records

declared gate input no call edge can reach (schema resources, config,
script, deps.edn, bb.edn, bin/test) runs every eligible test rather than

`seon.merge/merge!` takes a chain's terminal attempt as its source. That attempt's row lives on the chain branch, never on main. The change:
- `assignment-row` reads main's row, else the row of the chain branch that holds the attempt (new `chain-row`, over main's chain facts).
- The end and the task (`assigned-task`) are read on the source head.
- `prepare-merge!` takes a `:merging` option: root's facts merge (`merge-tx`) rides in the candidate's one write, so the tested world holds the source's tasks and attempts next to its program.
- The task is read on the source head only when a candidate is prepared, so a facts-only merge needs none. `chain-row` answers {} for a key no chain holds.
- In that write and in `accept-merge!`'s transaction, the facts go before the program: a program ref can name an entity the facts admit.
- One acceptance admits all the chain's tasks and attempts. The earlier attempts keep `:done`, the terminal one is `:merged`, and `my.root/merge-requests` lists none of them.

An agent's own namespace never merges (`seon.cluster.source/agent-owned` in `compare-branch`).
